hooks.text: One Soviet officer prevented a nuclear war by ignoring a missile warning.
What happens when satellites mistake sunlight for a nuclear strike?
Five incoming missiles appeared on Soviet screens at the height of the Cold War.

title: The officer who stopped World War III
description: On September 26, 1983, a Soviet early-warning system signaled a US missile attack, but one officer decided it was a false alarm.

beats.text: One Soviet officer prevented a nuclear war by ignoring a missile warning.
On September 26, 1983, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was the duty officer inside a secret Soviet nuclear bunker.
beats.visual: Cold war nuclear launch control panel in bunker, 1983
queries: Cold war command bunker control room

beats.text: Suddenly, the base’s early warning computer system reported a single incoming American missile.
beats.visual: Soviet Oko early warning satellite illustration, 1980s

beats.text: Moments later, the screens flashed again, identifying four additional missiles heading toward Moscow.
Soviet protocol demanded an immediate, compulsory nuclear counterattack to ensure the destruction of the United States.
beats.visual: Soviet military cold war command bunker control room, 1983

beats.text: But Petrov hesitated, reasoning that a real American first strike would involve hundreds of missiles, not just five.
beats.visual: Cold War Europe missile ranges map, 1983
queries: Cold War Europe missile ranges map

beats.text: Investigators later discovered that satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds for rocket exhaust.
beats.visual: Sunlight reflection on clouds satellite view, 1983
queries: sunlight reflection on clouds satellite view
